headline: Given each library's own documented workaround, almost the whole field converges on the static-class-plus-inline-style shape, which is what next-yak's compiler already emits from the obvious source.

microbench.why: Every lane here writes one static class and one inline style, so the ordering collapses to how much machinery still runs on top. `vanilla` (0.604 ms/1k), `next-yak-css-9.7` (0.617) and `bamboo` (0.633) are within noise of each other, and `cnfast` (0.640) and `tailwind-merge` (0.651) join them because a single repeated class list is a cache hit. next-yak's styled API stays at 1.23 ms/1k, twice its own inline-style figure, because the interpolation keeps a `Yak` runtime component on every element that folding would otherwise erase. `emotion` at 2.34 is the only lane still doing real per-instance work.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css-9.7` 1,290 req/s, `vanilla` 1,190, `cnfast` 1,160: the hand-split shape serves nearly twice what the naive one does for the same libraries. `styled-components` recovers to 622 req/s and `panda` to 543, both roughly triple their naive figures, since neither generates CSS per request any more.

attribution.why: `vanilla` (0.739 ms), `next-yak-css-9.7` (0.797) and `bamboo` (0.800) are react-dom plus one attribute write. What is left above them is each library's per-instance wrapper rather than any string work: `panda` 0.469 ms of component self-time reading its hoisted class constant, `stylex-layers` 0.311 ms of library plus 0.314 of component merging static atomic classes, and next-yak's styled API 0.704 ms of library because the dynamic interpolation reinstates the runtime component, 11.7 ms of it in the profile. `emotion` at 2.56 ms is alone in still serializing.

hydrate.why: 49.2-55.5 ms of pure JS for every lane whose sheet is finished, which is now nearly all of them, `styled-components` having dropped from injecting a thousand rules to injecting none. It still trails at 90.5 ms alongside `goober` (89.0) because both keep a sheet-management pass on the client; `emotion` at 77.1 ms re-serializes the static part.

inp.why: One element's transform changes, one style attribute is rewritten, and the entire field lands between 6.5 and 8.2 ms, a single measurement wide, with `emotion` at 10.7 the only lane outside it. Nothing distinguishes the libraries once the dynamic value stops touching the class name.

mount.why: 65.9-72.8 ms across the extracted, atomic and utility lanes. The lanes that were catastrophic in the naive case are ordinary here, `goober` at 86.1 ms and `styled-components` at 87.5 against their 1,320 and 116; `emotion` at 96.9 ms is the slowest, 1.47× the floor rather than twenty times it.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

renderTiming.why: One recalculation, one layout, one paint in every lane; the counts tie and recalc cost sits inside 0.105-0.189 ms for sixteen of the seventeen lanes, `next-yak-css-9.7`'s 1.12 ms being a single sample against its own 0.110 ms in the neighboring cases. Splitting the value out of the class name removes the only thing that could have made this measurement interesting.

payload.why: With the value out of the class name the stylesheet stops growing with the data: `next-yak-css-9.7` ships 105 B of CSS, `bamboo` 87 B, `emotion` 70 B. What remains is each library's runtime, and it dominates: `emotion` 12.9 kB of JS inside 18.3 total, `styled-components` 13.4 inside 18.9, `cnfast` 11.6 inside 17.0, against `next-yak-css-9.7`'s zero.

nsweep.why: `bamboo` (2.62 ms at n=4,000), `vanilla` (2.67) and `next-yak-css-9.7` (2.71) are flat and linear, and `cnfast` and `tailwind-merge` join them at 2.73 and 2.90. `emotion` at 9.96 ms is the only lane whose line still bends away from the floor, and `panda-props` at 7.28 the only other above 6.

crossCase: Set against the Example `dyn-translate` shown above, this case measures what developer discipline is worth: `goober` moves 5.98 to 1.06 ms/1k, `styled-components` 4.51 to 1.35, `panda` 4.87 to 1.15, `cnfast` 1.89 to 0.640, and cold mounts fall from 1,320 to 86.1 ms and 116 to 87.5 ms. Reaching parity means a person splits the static class from the dynamic inline style by hand, in every component, on every dynamic value, for the life of the codebase; next-yak ships that split as a compiler feature, which is why `next-yak-css-9.7` reads 0.596 and 0.617 ms/1k across the pair and had nothing to change. `bamboo` reaches the same shape from the other side, its compiler refusing to accept the naive spelling at all, so this file and its `dyn-translate` file are the same code. The Example `dyn-inline` shown below prices what next-yak's CSS-variable indirection itself costs against a plain inline style.
